item.title: The First Law
item.description:
Violent, dark, very graphic — and very well done. The character work is what kept me reading. In the second book everything starts to land. Around 60% through book two it grips hard if it hasn’t already.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_First_Law

item.title: The Three-Body Problem
item.description:
The Dark Forest, wallfacers and wallbreakers — great concepts. Worth the time.

Book two is the strongest of the trilogy. Book three felt like it could have lived in a different series — closer in tone to The Wandering Earth by the same author. It was hard to finish, but it’s good SF and asks the right questions.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Three-Body_Problem_(novel)

item.title: Expeditionary Force
item.description:
Skippy and Joe. The series starts as hard military SF, turns into very-well-done Star Trek, and eventually into its own thing.

There’s a mid-series detour into space opera that I’ll blame on Skippy. Some of the harder military fiction split off into its own series starting with Trouble on Paradise; the strategy and scheming stayed with Joe.

Plenty of pop-culture quips throughout, but the through-line is the same: work the problem in front of you.

item.title: Foundation
item.description:
Asimov runs through I, Robot, Bicentennial Man, and Foundation. I watched the screen adaptations long before tracing them back to the source.

Psycho-history is a fun premise. Worth reading.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foundation_series

item.title: Infinite
item.description:
Infinite and Infinite 2 are both good. Several of Jeremy Robinson’s other novels (Torment, others) tie in as crossovers from Infinite 3 onward.

If you only read two, read 1 and 2. The rest are fun but lighter on the heavy questions.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Robinson

item.title: Red Rising
item.description:
Read the whole series and recommend it. The original trilogy in particular has some sharp ideas worth sitting with.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Rising
